analogy.p: A cook follows a recipe, tastes the result (testing), and then refines it: fixing mistakes such as too much salt (correctness), cutting out an unnecessary step to save time (efficiency), adding a note so a guest with an allergy is not harmed (robustness), and rewriting it in clear steps with headings so anyone can follow it (readability). After each change the cook tastes the dish again (retesting) to make sure the change helped and nothing else went wrong. The analogy breaks down because a computer can repeat a test thousands of times instantly and cheaply, and a software change can break something completely unrelated in a way a recipe change never could.
analogy.t: Editing a recipe after tasting the dish

bullets: Know that refining is **improving a working or partly working algorithm** after testing or review.
Be able to give **reasons**: correctness, efficiency, robustness, readability and maintainability.
Be able to suggest **concrete changes**: loops instead of repeated code, early exit, `elseif`, subprograms, validation, comments, meaningful names.
Know that refining is part of the **iterative cycle**: test, find faults, refine, retest.
Be able to **compare** a basic and a refined version of an algorithm and say why one is better.
Links to **testing** (2.3.2), **defensive design** (2.3.1), **maintainability** (2.3.1), **sorting and searching** (2.1).
Exam answers need **specific, code-linked suggestions**, not just 'make it better'.
core.p: Within OCR J277 section 2.3 (producing robust programs) you are expected to understand that an algorithm is rarely perfect first time and must be **refined**, meaning improved after testing and review. Refining can mean correcting faults the tests exposed, making the program **more efficient** (fewer steps or less memory), **more robust** (able to cope with unexpected input) and **easier to read and maintain**. You may be asked to explain why an algorithm should be refined, to suggest specific improvements to a given piece of code or pseudocode, or to identify a better version of an algorithm. It links strongly to testing, because the results of testing are what tell you what to refine.

bullets: Refining = **improving** an algorithm or program **without changing its purpose** (unless the purpose was wrongly specified).
It happens **during development** (iterative testing) and after **final testing**, and again later as part of maintenance.
The **inputs and expected outputs stay the same**; what changes is how the result is reached or how the code is written.
Refinement is driven by **evidence**: test results, user feedback, timing, code review.
The refined version must still pass **all the earlier tests** (regression testing).
Refinement is not a sign of failure: **professional programmers refine constantly**.
Stepwise refinement is also a design term (breaking a general step into more detailed steps); here the focus is **improving an existing algorithm**.
core.p: To **refine** an algorithm is to go back to a solution that already exists and improve it. The first version of an algorithm usually concentrates on simply getting the right answer; refinement then asks whether it can be made **faster, shorter, safer or clearer** without changing what it is supposed to achieve. Testing is the trigger: tests may show wrong results, slow performance, crashes on odd input, or code that is difficult to follow. Each refinement is then **retested**, because a change that improves one thing can accidentally break another.

bullets: Use the **test plan**: any row where **actual result is not the expected result** points to a refinement.
**Boundary data** often exposes a wrong comparison (`>` should be `>=`).
**Invalid data** exposes missing checks, leading to **validation** being added.
**Logic errors** (wrong formula, wrong loop range) are corrected in the algorithm itself.
**Syntax errors** are fixed so the program can be translated and run.
After correcting, **retest every test**, not only the failed one.
Record each change so you can **explain what was altered and why**.
core.h: Reason 1: refine to make the algorithm correct
core.p: The first and most important reason to refine is to remove faults found in testing, because a program that gives wrong results is useless however fast it is. Tests with **normal, boundary and invalid data** compare the expected and actual results, and every mismatch reveals something to correct. Typical corrections are changing an operator, fixing a loop's start or end value, moving a statement, or adding a missing case. Once fixed, you retest to prove the fault has gone.

bullets: **Stop early** (exit a loop) once the answer is found, e.g. a linear search that stops at the first match.
**Avoid repeated work**: calculate a value once, store it in a variable and reuse it, instead of recalculating inside a loop.
**Use `elseif` / selection properly** so conditions are not all tested when one already matched.
**Reduce the number of passes**: e.g. a bubble sort that shortens each pass and stops when no swaps happen.
**Choose a better algorithm**: binary search instead of linear search on sorted data; merge sort instead of bubble sort for large lists.
**Use fewer variables or smaller data structures** if memory is limited (e.g. embedded systems).
Efficiency matters most for **large data sets** and **time-critical** programs; for a tiny list the saving may be invisible.
Efficiency may be traded against **readability**: the clearest version is not always the fastest.
core.h: Reason 2: refine to make the algorithm more efficient
core.p: An **efficient** algorithm uses fewer resources: fewer **steps** (so it runs faster) and less **memory**. Two algorithms can give identical answers yet one may take a fraction of the time, and the difference becomes huge as the amount of data grows. Efficiency is improved by removing unnecessary work, stopping as soon as the answer is known, avoiding repeated calculations and choosing a better algorithm for the job.

bullets: **Basic version** on 5 items: 4 passes x 4 comparisons = **16 comparisons**, even if already sorted.
**Shorter inner loop** (ignore items already in place): 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = **10 comparisons**.
**Swapped flag** on an already sorted list: one pass of 4 comparisons, no swaps, so it stops = **4 comparisons**.
Pseudocode idea: `swapped = true` / `while swapped == true` / `swapped = false` / inside the loop set `swapped = true` after each swap.
The flag version is also faster on **nearly sorted** lists, which are common in real data.
In the **worst case** (list in reverse order) the refinement does not help much, so it is an **improvement, not a cure**.
Remember the answer stays the same: the list ends up **sorted**; only the **work done** changes.
core.h: Refining a bubble sort: a worked efficiency case
core.p: Bubble sort works by repeatedly comparing neighbouring items and swapping them if they are in the wrong order. A basic version always does **n - 1 passes**, and each pass makes **n - 1 comparisons**, even if the list is already sorted. Two simple refinements make it much quicker: after each pass the largest item is in its final place, so the **next pass can be one comparison shorter**, and a **flag** (for example `swapped`) records whether any swap happened, so the algorithm can **stop as soon as a whole pass has no swaps**. For a sorted list of 5 items this reduces the comparisons from 16 to 10 to just 4.

bullets: **Linear search with early exit**: target 15 at position 3 in a list of 8 needs **3 comparisons** instead of 8.
Use a **flag**, e.g. `found = false`, and loop `while found == false AND index < length`.
**Binary search** needs the list to be **sorted first**; it checks the **middle item** and discards half each time.
Worst case for 1000 items: **linear 1000** comparisons, **binary 10** comparisons.
Binary search is **not always better**: if the list is unsorted you must pay the cost of sorting it first.
If you only search once, a linear search may be the more sensible choice.
Both algorithms must still be **tested** with the item at the start, middle, end and not present.
core.h: Refining searches: early exit and choosing the right algorithm
core.p: A **linear search** checks items one at a time from the start. A weak version carries on to the end of the list even after the item is found, wasting effort, so a simple refinement is to **stop the loop as soon as a match is found**, for example by using a `found` flag in the loop condition. A far bigger improvement is switching to a **binary search** when the data is **already sorted**: it halves the search area every step. For 1000 sorted items a linear search may need up to 1000 comparisons, but a binary search needs at most 10, because 2^10 = 1024 is just over 1000.

bullets: Add **input validation**: range checks, type checks, presence checks, length checks, format checks.
Add **authentication**: ask the user to prove their identity (e.g. username and password) before giving access.
Add **input sanitisation** so unwanted characters or code are removed from what the user types.
Add **clear error messages** and repeat the input request until valid data is entered (a validation loop).
Anticipate misuse: think about **what the worst input could be** and plan for it.
Add **error handling** for missing files or impossible calculations such as dividing by zero.
After adding validation, test with **normal, boundary, invalid and erroneous** data again.
core.h: Reason 3: refine to make the program more robust
core.p: A **robust** program keeps working sensibly even when given unexpected, invalid or hostile input. Testing with invalid and erroneous data often shows the program crashing or accepting nonsense, so the algorithm is refined to include **defensive design** features. The idea is to expect mistakes from users and deal with them politely rather than failing.

bullets: **Meaningful identifier names**: `totalPrice` rather than `x`.
**Comments** that explain **why** the code does something, not only what it does.
**Indentation and white space** to show the structure of loops and selection.
**Subprograms (procedures and functions)** so a task is written once and reused, and so the program is split into manageable chunks.
**Constants** for fixed values such as `VAT = 0.2`, so a change needs editing in one place only.
**Consistent style** and avoiding overly clever one-line tricks.
**Reduce repeated code** by using loops and subprograms.
core.h: Reason 4: refine to improve readability and maintainability
core.p: Even if the code works and is fast, it may be hard for another programmer (or you in six months) to understand. **Maintainable** code is easy to read, fix and extend. The specification lists specific habits that make code maintainable, and refining often means going back and adding them. Readable code has fewer errors, because mistakes are easier to spot.

bullets: **Before**: five lines `mark1 = int(input())` ... `mark5 = int(input())` and a long addition.
**After**: `total = 0`, `for i = 1 to 5`, `total = total + int(input("Mark"))`, `next i`.
The loop version can be changed to 30 marks by altering **one number**; the repeated version needs 25 more lines.
A **function** returns a value to the caller; a **procedure** does a task and does not return a value.
Subprograms can be **tested separately**, which makes debugging easier.
Use **parameters** to pass data into a subprogram rather than relying on global variables.
Shorter code is not automatically better: it must remain **clear**.
core.h: Using loops and subprograms to remove repetition
core.p: A common refinement is to replace several almost identical lines with a **loop**, or to turn a repeated block of code into a **subprogram** that is called whenever it is needed. This makes the program shorter, less error-prone and far easier to change, because a fix is made in one place. For example, five separate input and add statements can become a `for` loop that runs five times, and the same calculation used in three places can become a function.

bullets: **Before**: `if mark >= 70 then`, `if mark >= 60 and mark < 70 then`, `if mark >= 50 and mark < 60 then` each tested separately.
**After**: `if mark >= 70 then` / `elseif mark >= 60 then` / `elseif mark >= 50 then` / `else`.
The refined version has **fewer conditions to write** and no overlapping range tests.
Mark 80: **basic = 3 checks, refined = 1 check**.
Mark 65: basic = 3 checks; refined = 2 checks (fails the first, matches the second).
An `else` at the end catches **everything not matched**, helping robustness.
A `select case` (switch) statement can be used for a long list of exact values.
core.h: Refining with selection: elseif instead of separate ifs
core.p: Another very common exam example is a series of separate `if` statements where only one can be true. Written separately, the computer checks **every** condition even after one has matched, and the conditions often need extra tests such as `and mark < 70` to avoid overlapping. Refining this to a single `if ... elseif ... else` structure means checking stops at the first true condition, the conditions are simpler, and the code is easier to read. For a mark of 80, the basic version makes 3 checks and the refined version just 1.

bullets: The cycle: **write, test, find faults, refine, retest**.
**Iterative testing** catches problems early when they are cheaper to fix.
**Regression testing**: rerun old tests after a change to make sure nothing else broke.
**Final testing** uses a full set of test data on the **whole program**.
Keep a **test log**: what was tested, expected, actual, what was changed.
Use **version control or backups** so you can revert a bad refinement.
Stop refining when the program **meets the requirements** and further changes are not worth the effort.
core.h: Refining as part of iterative testing
core.p: Refinement does not happen once; it forms part of a cycle that repeats until the program meets its requirements. You test, find a problem, **refine** the algorithm, then **retest**, and each loop of the cycle should leave the program better. Alongside **iterative testing** (done while developing, module by module) there is **final or terminal testing** on the finished product, which may trigger further refinements. Keeping a record of each version and change helps if a refinement makes things worse and you need to go back.

bullets: **Efficiency vs readability**: a clever one-liner can be quick but hard to understand.
**Memory vs speed**: storing a result uses memory but saves recalculation.
**Decomposition**: refine one **module at a time** and test it separately.
**Abstraction**: a function's inside can be improved without changing how it is called.
**Defensive design** (2.3.1): validation, authentication and anticipating misuse are all refinements.
**Embedded systems** have limited memory, so efficiency in memory use matters more.
**Do not over-refine**: improvements should have a purpose, not just change code.
core.h: Trade-offs, limits and links to other topics
core.p: Refinement always involves judgement. Faster code can be harder to read, shorter code can be harder to debug, and extra validation makes a program longer. A good answer shows awareness of these trade-offs, saying which improvement suits the situation, such as memory savings for an embedded system or readability for a team project. Link refinement to **decomposition** (breaking a problem into smaller parts that can each be refined), **abstraction** (hiding detail so a subprogram can be improved without the rest of the program changing) and **defensive design** (anticipating misuse).

bullets: Use the pattern **change + reason**: 'use a loop (1) so repeated code is removed (1)'.
For **efficiency**, quote **numbers of comparisons or steps** if the question gives data.
For **readability**, name two or three techniques: comments, indentation, meaningful names, subprograms.
For **robustness**, name validation types and say what they prevent.
For **discuss** questions, offer both a **benefit and a drawback** (e.g. longer code, more testing).
For **Compare two algorithms**, state which is better **and why** in a given situation.
Always mention **retesting** after any change if the question is about the process.
core.p: Refinement questions reward specific, reasoned suggestions that fit the code in front of you. Generic answers such as 'make it more efficient' or 'make it better' earn no marks, whereas 'replace the repeated lines with a for loop so the code is shorter and easier to maintain' earns full credit. Always name the change, link it to the code, and give the benefit.

exam: **Command words**: 'State' (1 mark, short), 'Describe/Explain' (link the change to a reason), 'Discuss' (benefits and drawbacks), 'Compare' (similarity and difference with a conclusion).
**Typical 2-mark question**: 'Give one way the code could be refined.' Answer: 'use a loop instead of repeated statements (1) so the code is shorter / easier to maintain (1)'.
**Structure for refinement answers**: change (1) + reason or benefit (1); repeat for each point asked.
**Efficiency**: refer to **fewer steps, fewer comparisons, faster execution or less memory**; use the figures given in the question.
**Readability / maintainability**: choose from comments, meaningful variable names, indentation, subprograms, constants; avoid saying just 'neat'.
**Robustness**: name the check (range, type, length, presence, format), say what it stops, and mention a loop that asks the user to re-enter.
**Sorting / searching refinements**: early exit, swapped flag, shortening the pass, binary search for sorted data. Always say why it saves work.
**3-4 mark 'explain why a programmer would refine a working program'**: efficiency, robustness, readability, then 'retest after changes' as a final point.
**6-mark discuss**: give at least two reasons for refining, one example of code change each, a drawback or trade-off, and a conclusion.
**Show trade-offs** to reach the top band: 'although the refined code is faster, it takes more testing / is harder to read'.
**Link to testing**: say that results of testing (expected versus actual) tell the programmer **what** to refine.
**Avoid vague words**: 'better', 'quicker' and 'easier' need a reason from the code.

mistakes.r: Name the specific change and its benefit: 'use a for loop instead of repeated lines to reduce code and make it easier to maintain'.
mistakes.w: 'Make the code better' or 'make it run faster'.

mistakes.r: Refining improves how the algorithm works (correctness, efficiency, robustness, readability); the intended outputs stay the same.
mistakes.w: Refining changes what the program is meant to do.

mistakes.r: A passing program can still be refined for efficiency, robustness and readability, and must be retested after any change.
mistakes.w: Once a test passes, no more changes are needed.

mistakes.r: Binary search only works on sorted data; if the list is unsorted it must be sorted first.
mistakes.w: A binary search can always be used instead of linear search.

mistakes.r: Efficiency is about fewer steps or less memory; shorter code can still be slow, and very compact code may be harder to read.
mistakes.w: Shorter code is always more efficient.

mistakes.r: Validation checks only that data is sensible and in the allowed form; it does not guarantee it is correct.
mistakes.w: Validation makes sure the data is correct.

mistakes.r: Comments are ignored by the translator; they make the code easier to read and maintain.
mistakes.w: Comments make the program run faster.

mistakes.r: Always retest, including earlier tests (regression testing), to check nothing else has broken.

summary: The specification asks you to understand that algorithms are refined after testing: corrected so they work, made more efficient (fewer steps or less memory), more robust (able to cope with invalid input) and more readable and maintainable. It matters because Paper 2 asks you to suggest and justify specific improvements to code and to explain how testing and retesting drive them.

terms.d: Improving an existing algorithm or program, for example to correct errors or to make it more efficient, robust or readable.
How well an algorithm uses resources such as processing time (number of steps) and memory.
Able to cope with unexpected, invalid or erroneous input without crashing or giving wrong results.
Easy to understand, correct and update, because of features such as comments, meaningful names, indentation and subprograms.
Repeated testing during development, where faults are found, fixed and retested as the program is built.
Testing the completed program, with a full range of test data, to check it meets its requirements.
Re-running earlier tests after a change to check that the change has not broken anything that previously worked.
Leaving a loop as soon as the result is known, so unnecessary repetitions are avoided.
A variable, often Boolean, used to record whether something has happened, such as swapped or found.
A named block of code (a procedure or function) that carries out a task and can be called from elsewhere.
A subprogram that returns a value to the part of the program that called it.
A subprogram that carries out a task but does not return a value.
Automatic checking that data entered is reasonable and sensible; it does not prove the data is correct.
Confirming that a user is who they claim to be, for example with a username and password.
Text in the code ignored by the translator that explains what the code does or why, to help programmers.
A named value that is set once and cannot change while the program runs.
Breaking a complex problem down into smaller, more manageable parts.

worked.ans: (a) 25 comparisons (1). (b) 5 comparisons (1), because the algorithm stops after one pass with no swaps (1).
worked.q: A bubble sort is used on a list of 6 items that is already in order. The basic algorithm always makes every pass and compares neighbouring pairs on each pass. (a) Work out the number of comparisons made by the basic algorithm. (b) The programmer adds a flag called swapped so that the algorithm stops when a pass makes no swaps. How many comparisons are made now? [3]
steps: For n = 6 items, each pass compares 5 neighbouring pairs (n - 1 = 5).
The basic algorithm makes n - 1 = 5 passes, so 5 x 5 = 25 comparisons.
With the flag: the first pass makes 5 comparisons and no swaps occur, so swapped remains false and the algorithm stops.
So the refined version makes 5 comparisons, 20 fewer.

worked.ans: Use if ... elseif ... else (1) so checking stops at the first true condition (1). Mark 80: 3 checks before, 1 check after (1). Benefit: more efficient and easier to read/maintain (1).
worked.q:
The following OCR pseudocode converts a mark to a grade.
if mark >= 70 then grade = "A" endif
if mark >= 60 and mark < 70 then grade = "B" endif
if mark >= 50 and mark < 60 then grade = "C" endif
Explain how the code could be refined and state one benefit. How many conditions are checked for a mark of 80 before and after? [4]
steps: Replace the three separate if statements with one if ... elseif structure.
Because later conditions are only checked when earlier ones are false, the extra tests mark < 70 and mark < 60 are no longer needed.
Before: for mark 80 all three conditions are evaluated = 3 checks.
After: the first condition is true, so the rest are skipped = 1 check.
Benefits: fewer checks, shorter conditions and easier to read.

worked.ans: To improve speed, remove repeated calculations or use loops that exit early / a more efficient algorithm such as binary search on sorted data (2). To make it readable, add comments, meaningful variable names, indentation and split the code into subprograms (2). To stop it crashing, add a type check validation so that letters are rejected with an error message and the user is asked to re-enter (1). Finally, retest the program with normal, boundary and invalid data to make sure the changes work and nothing has broken (1).
worked.q: A programmer's program passes all of its tests but runs slowly, is difficult for others to read and crashes if the user types letters instead of a number. Describe how the programmer could refine the program. [6]
steps: Pick three areas: efficiency, readability/maintainability, robustness.
Efficiency: use early exit, avoid repeating calculations, use a more suitable algorithm.
Readability: comments, meaningful names, indentation, subprograms.
Robustness: type check validation inside a loop with an error message.
